posts.copy:
Hesai's lidar shipments rose 78.4% in the second quarter of 2026. Its revenue rose 21.9%.

That gap is the story, and it is not a weak quarter.

Hesai shipped 628,275 lidar units in those three months. 142,371 of them were for robotics rather than cars, up 193.4% on a year earlier. Net revenue was RMB860.8 million, and the quarter was profitable.

Read from a desk in London or San Francisco, units racing ahead of revenue looks like a price war, and the comfortable conclusion is to wait for it to burn out.

That reading gets the fact right and the meaning wrong. A sensor that gets cheaper every quarter stops being only a car part and starts being a robot part. That is what the robotics line shows. The cost curve moved, and a new set of buyers appeared underneath it.

A results table cannot show you that loop. In China's hardware clusters the robot makers buying these sensors sit close to the people making them, and a cheaper part turns into a new product faster than a Western roadmap expects.

The ecosystem is the product, not the company. Falling prices are how a component finds its next market.

posts.copy:
1,975 robotaxis. That was the global fleet Pony.ai reported in its second-quarter 2026 results.

The fleet is not the news. The fares are.

In that quarter Pony.ai's robotaxi revenue reached US$12.1 million, up 691.2% on a year earlier, and fare-charging revenue rose 849.3%. Total revenue was US$36.2 million, up 68.8%, while the net loss narrowed 14.9% to US$45.4 million.

Read from a desk in New York or Munich, driverless ride-hailing still looks like a science project that will burn cash for another decade. These numbers describe something else: a paid service, still loss-making, growing far faster than its losses.

The reason is not one clever model. A robotaxi fleet is a hardware problem as much as a software one. Every new car needs sensors, compute and a vehicle to put them in, and in China the suppliers for all three already build at electric-vehicle volumes.

That is the part you cannot read in an earnings release. The software gets the headlines. The speed comes from how close the parts are.

The ecosystem is the product, not the company.

posts.copy:
Nobody wants to hear this, but China's energy-storage boom came with a warning from its own regulator.

In October 2026 China's industry ministry said energy-storage battery output exceeded 420 gigawatt-hours in the first half of 2026, up 110% on a year earlier. Overseas orders signed in those six months reached 298 GWh, up 83%.

In the same speech the vice minister called on the industry to resolutely prevent "involution-style" competition. That is the official phrase for price wars and overcapacity.

Read from Europe, the reflex is to pick one half. Either China is about to own grid storage, or it is a bubble about to pop. Both are true at once, and the useful question is which suppliers come out the other side.

A production statistic cannot answer that. It gets answered in conversations with the cell makers, the system integrators and the buyers behind those overseas orders, by working out who is pricing for share and who is pricing to last.

That is the kind of ground our OJV Educate tours for executives are built to cover.

posts.copy:
In May 2018 Walmart agreed to pay about $16 billion for roughly 77% of Flipkart. Here is what that bought that building could not:

Walmart did not launch its own Indian marketplace. It bought an Indian company that already had the customers, the sellers and the team.

→ The team stayed. Walmart's announcement said Flipkart's leadership would be supported by Walmart, alongside Tencent, Tiger Global and Microsoft.

→ The money went into the business too. The deal included $2 billion of new equity funding.

→ The company moved home. In March 2026 Flipkart completed its redomiciliation to India.

This is not a victory lap. In the year to March 2026 Flipkart's revenue rose 18% to Rs 1.46 lakh crore, and it still made a consolidated net loss of Rs 8,468 crore. In May 2026 it put its planned IPO on hold.

What the deal shows is a choice. In a market that size and that local, Walmart decided time was worth more than building from zero.

In some of APAC's 15+ ecosystems the fastest way in is a partner or an acquisition, not a launch. Working out which ones is a large part of go-to-market work.

We have never worked with Walmart or Flipkart. This is commentary from the outside.

posts.copy:
Would you bet against Apple in India because it arrived late? Its first stores of its own there opened in 2023.

Apple's retail presence in India began that year with Apple BKC in Mumbai and Apple Saket in Delhi. In February 2026 Apple Borivali opened as its second store in Mumbai and its sixth in India.

Between those openings, on the October 2025 earnings call, Tim Cook, then chief executive, said Apple had set an all-time revenue record in India.

The unlock was distribution it owned, sitting on a supply chain that had moved closer. India's iPhone exports reached Rs 2 trillion in the eleven months to February 2026, up from Rs 1.5 trillion in the previous financial year.

What Apple did not do was rush the shopfront. Six stores in three years is a handful of flagships, not a land grab.

Market entry is not one decision. Distribution, price and supply each have their own order, and that order is different in each of APAC's 15+ ecosystems. Getting it right matters more than getting there first.

Mapping that order is where our GTM advisory work starts.

We have never worked with Apple. This is commentary from the outside.

posts.copy:
Uber's way into Japan was to stop being Uber.

In 2015 Japanese authorities ordered Uber to halt its ridesharing pilot in Fukuoka, citing legal and regulatory issues.

In December 2020 Uber Japan signed a partnership with the taxi operator Hinomaru Kotsu, and the two agreed to oppose illegal ridesharing. From then on, Uber in Japan meant licensed taxis booked through the app.

By the end of 2025 Uber Taxi ran in all 47 prefectures, two years ahead of its 2027 target, with more than 1,000 partner taxi companies. That is according to the head of Uber Japan, who said in a February 2026 interview that it had grown at roughly double each year for about three years.

The unlock was regulatory sequencing. Uber did not fight the licensing system. It plugged into it. The drivers, cars and licences stayed with local operators, and Uber brought the demand.

In plenty of APAC's 15+ ecosystems the regulation is the market structure. The entrant that works through local licences gets to scale. The one that argues with them gets a pilot.

Sequencing is the first thing we map in a GTM advisory engagement, before positioning and before pricing.

We have never worked with Uber or Hinomaru Kotsu. This is commentary from the outside.

posts.copy:
106 investor rejections came before Ukhi's first institutional round. Its co-founder counted every one.

Vishal Vivek wrote the number down himself in April 2026. Ukhi, founded in India in 2019, makes compostable biomaterials. It was a biomaterials company at the first no and at the yes.

What changed was this.

The pitch narrowed. He had been pitching a broad range of hemp applications. In his words, "The turning point came when I stripped the pitch down to one product, one market and one clear path to scale."

The route in changed. His first angel investment, he wrote, "didn't come from a cold email." It came through a recommendation from the IIT Mandi Catalyst incubator.

Then the rounds. In November 2024 Ukhi raised $1.2 million in a pre-seed round led by 100Unicorns. In February 2026 it raised Rs 10.5 crore in a seed round led by Venture Catalysts.

106 nos to a pitch that tried to be everything is not a verdict on the company. It is information about the pitch and the list.

That is the part of fundraising support we do. We tighten the story, cut the list and work the warm paths. We do not promise the yes, because nobody honest can.

We have never worked with Ukhi. This is commentary from the outside.

posts.copy:
American shoppers are supposed to buy clothes on sale. Uniqlo stopped discounting there.

The product was never the problem. Uniqlo spent 17 years in the US before, in 2022, it was poised to book its first annual profit in North America.

What it changed was the price and the story.

The price. "Our competitors offer discounts of 50 per cent or 60 per cent, but we have basically stopped that," its North America chief told Reuters in September 2022. Fast Retailing later described reviewing prices and reducing discounting to lift margins there.

The story. It opened large flagship stores that it calls media beacons, built to raise brand awareness and push e-commerce sales.

In the year to August 2026, North America revenue rose 34.6% to 364.9 billion yen, and business profit rose 53.3% to 67.9 billion yen. For the first time, North America and Europe together outsold Greater China.

The hard part was never the shirts. It was teaching a new buyer to pay full price, and telling them why.

That is the order our GTM advisory work follows for Asian companies moving West: the buyer, the pricing, then the story.

We were not involved in Uniqlo's expansion. This is commentary.

posts.copy:
Asian beauty brands call US retail the prize, then start by chasing it. Medicube reached the American shelf last.

APR, the Korean company behind Medicube, built US demand online first, through marketplaces and TikTok Shop, adjusting its products and sales strategy for each channel.

Then the stores. About 1,400 Ulta Beauty stores in 2025. More than 1,500 Target stores in April 2026. Costco shelves in October 2026.

The numbers moved with it. The US was 22% of APR's sales in 2024 and 37% in 2025, a year in which its overseas revenue rose 207% to KRW 1.23 trillion. In the first half of 2026 its North American sales reached 647.9 billion won.

The products were already selling. What changed was which buyer saw the evidence first. A chain's buyer was not asked to take a bet on an unknown Korean brand. The online sales were the pitch.

That is the pattern in most Asia-to-West moves. The hard part is rarely the product. It is the buyer you convince first, the price they compare you against, and the story they need before they put their name on it.

We have never worked with APR or Medicube. This is commentary from the outside.

posts.copy:
Give us an hour with a hardware company selling into APAC and we can usually tell which link in the chain is costing it the market.

We start with four things:

→ Certification
→ Channel
→ Landed price
→ Service

Then we look at what is underneath them.

Do you know which certifications each market needs before a distributor will even take the meeting, or are you finding out one rejection at a time?

Who holds your stock? A distributor carrying ten competing brands has no reason to push yours.

Is your price set from your factory cost, or from what the product actually lands at after duty, freight and the channel's margin?

When a unit fails three time zones away, who fixes it, and how many days does the customer wait?

From the inside, a slow hardware market looks like weak demand. Sometimes it is. More often the product never reached the shelf at a price and a service level the buyer could say yes to, and a better product does not fix that.

APAC is not one market. It is 15+ ecosystems with different rules, cultures and buyer behaviour, so the job is rapid recalibration, not a rigid playbook.

If you are selling hardware into APAC and your distributors have gone quiet, work with us.

DM us, or write to us at hello@oj.ventures
